title: A buffalo recites the Veda
hookLine: four children turned away, and a buffalo that recites the Veda
carry: atman: the same self lives in every being
tomorrow: The Gita in the people's language

cards: Four children walk into a town of learned Brahmins with a request. Three brothers and a little sister, shut out by their community their whole lives, through no fault of their own. They want to be accepted.
The scholars look them over and start to laugh. One points at a buffalo plodding by, and makes a joke about names.
Today the path moves north and west, into the Marathi-speaking country, and meets the second of those children: Jnaneshwar.

teach.b: Here's the story as tradition tells it. The children's father had left home to become a sannyasi, a renunciant. His teacher sent him back home.
To their community, a monk who goes home has broken the order of things, and the family is cast out. Four children are born into that: Nivritti, Jnanadev, Sopan, and their sister Muktabai.
Before long, the story says, they're on their own.
So they go to the Brahmins of Paithan to ask for a letter of purification that would let them belong.
Hearing the second boy's name, Jnanadev, which carries the Sanskrit word for knowledge, someone mocks him: names mean nothing; look, that buffalo has a name too. Jnaneshwar doesn't argue.
The story says he answers that the same Self lives in the buffalo as in him, and places his hand on its head.

teach.h: THE VEDA FROM AN ANIMAL'S MOUTH.
teach.b: And the buffalo begins to recite the Veda, the text these men spent their lives learning. The scholars fall silent, and some tellings say they then grant the letter.
This is one of Hinduism's biggest teachings, acted out in a street.

teach.h: ATMAN: THE SAME SELF IN EVERY BEING.
teach.b: The Upanishads call it atman: the Self, the deepest you, is one and the same in every being, a scholar, an outcast child, a buffalo.
If that's true, the line between those worth hearing and those who don't count was never real.
And the Varkari path that honors Jnaneshwar came to include saints who were a tailor, a potter, a maidservant, and Chokhamela, whose caste was treated as untouchable.

how: Jnaneshwar is honored across Maharashtra, especially by the Varkari tradition; his shrine is at Alandi, and stories of his childhood, including the buffalo at Paithan, are told and staged by devotees.

o: the Brahmin scholar of Paithan who mocked the children
the Marathi poet-saint who made a buffalo recite the Veda
the father who left home and then came back from the monks

games.q: the story at Paithan — tap the pairs.
p: the same Self in every being

s: the family was shut out for something the children did
they were cast out because their father, a renunciant, went back to household life.
Jnaneshwar answered the mockery with an argument
he said the same Self lives in the buffalo, and touched its head.
one telling says the whip marks rose on the boy's back
when the buffalo was whipped, the marks appeared on him.

games.q: you're Jnaneshwar. a scholar sneers that your name means nothing, since even that buffalo has a name. what do you do?
o: recite the Veda yourself to prove your learning.
say the same Self lives in the buffalo, and touch its head.
walk away and never come back.
games.why: he puts his hand on the buffalo's head, and the story says the buffalo begins to recite the Veda: the same Self, atman, in an outcast boy and an animal.

practice: Bring to mind a creature you rarely think about, a pigeon, a stray dog, an insect, breathing too. Then add a person you tend to look past. Hold them both, and say quietly: the same Self in you as in me.
If you pray, hold them before God in words you already use. If you don't, just let them both stay.

wordCard.voice: Jnaneshwar. Also called Jnanadev. The Marathi poet-saint who, the story says, made a buffalo recite the Veda to answer the people who shut his family out.

orig.note: Marathi, in Devanagari: the name of the saint, which carries the Sanskrit word for knowledge.

carryVoice: Your line: atman, the same self lives in every being. Tomorrow: what happens when the Gita leaves Sanskrit? Day nine hundred thirteen, done.
